title: WWF in 2025: A year of progress for people and planet

sections.heading: Body
sections.text:
Posted on December, 22 2025
Safe passage along migratory highways are crucial for maintaining healthy populations of whales. © naturepl.com / Mary McDonald / WWF
WWF reflects on the efforts made by many in 2025 to secure a better world for all life on Earth.
WWF has been working alongside partners and supporters around the world for over 60 years, achieving many incredible conservation wins while also, sometimes, enduring disappointing setbacks along the way.
And so 2025 has proved to be a year like so many others – a year of soaring highs but also one of dispiriting lows.
New global initiatives on oceans, forests and more are proof positive of the progress we can make together. And our ambitious plan over the coming five years to help reverse nature loss and stabilize the climate is gaining momentum.
However, the year showed that many obstacles still lie in our way – from fragmented approaches taken by governments around the world to the spiralling misinformation infecting public debate.
Here at WWF, we remain a beacon of hope – combining an unwavering sense of purpose and determination to act with a growing ability to solve the many diverse and complex challenges.
2026 will offer new beginnings for those of us, WWF included, who want to build a better future for all. The journey ahead will be far from smooth. But together, we can deliver the change so desperately needed for life on Earth.
As we prepare for the coming crucial year, let’s look back at some of the progress we’ve made together in the past 12 months:
Ocean breakthrough
The effort of WWF and others helped secure commitments at this year’s UN Ocean Conference to create over 500 million hectares of marine protected areas, meaning that once implemented, more than 10 per cent of the ocean will be protected. The event also saw an impressive €8.7 billion committed to ocean conservation.
In other good news, the WWF-backed high seas treaty was ratified by the 60 countries needed to ensure it comes into force in January 2026 – finally, there will be a legally binding mechanism for creating protected areas and acting against harmful activities in areas beyond national control. And we supported the launch of BlueCorridors.org, a global platform mapping whale migration routes and marine threats.
Tropical forests provide many of the things we rely on daily. © César David Martinez
Forest game changer
The new WWF-backed Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) is set to be the biggest fund ever to support tropical forest conservation. The TFFF aims to raise US$125 billion from governments and private investors to create an investment fund that will channel an anticipated US$4 billion each year into keeping forests standing. While we welcome that over US$6.5 billion in investments were announced at this year’s UN COP30 climate conference, we must now work for more governments and investors to support the facility.
Restoring nature
It’s been two years since the UN agreement by countries around the world to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030. WWF is proud to have played our part in making this happen but is also concerned about the desperate need for action. At this year’s UN biodiversity conference, we helped coordinate an 18-country Champions Group, which called for targets to be set across all sectors of the global economy and pushed for a stronger finance system to help pay for biodiversity action. Progress has been made but more hard work is still needed to make this all become a reality.
COP30 promised much – but didn’t deliver the decisive steps the world urgently needs. © Jacqueline Lisboa / WWF-Brazil
Climate progress
Work on climate and energy continued under challenging geopolitics. Globally, fossil-fuel CO2 emissions reached record highs; but renewable energy also surpassed coal as the world’s biggest source of electricity in the first half of 2025. This year’s UN COP30 climate conference didn’t provide the global unity of purpose WWF is striving for but many governments agreed on the need for coordinated action against fossil fuels and deforestation – the coming year will see efforts by WWF and others to make this a reality. Signs of progress also came from judicial decisions, including a landmark advisory opinion on climate change from the International Court of Justice – recognizing that states have obligations to avoid harmful impacts from greenhouse gas emissions to the climate system and to nature.
Community-led conservation
Indigenous Peoples and local communities have a vital role in building a sustainable future for life on Earth. So we strongly supported the Brazzaville Declaration, which emphasizes the crucial role of Indigenous Peoples in managing and preserving the rich biodiversity of the world’s three largest forest basins. The declaration was made by representatives from around round the world, ahead of the first Global Congress of Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities of the Forest Basins. Also in 2025, WWF’s new People Powering Biodiversity project is helping to accelerate efforts to halt and reverse nature loss through community-led conservation. The CHF15 million initiative spans WWF offices in Papua New Guinea, Republic of Congo, Tanzania, Tunisia and Viet Nam.
From iconic landmarks to small communities, Earth Hour’s signature switch-off moment was observed across the globe. ©ThinkMammoth
Earth Hour
Millions came together for WWF’s Earth Hour on Saturday, 22 March, in an inspiring show of unity and commitment to our planet − reminding us all that we need to act together against the climate and nature loss crises. Individuals, communities and organizations in over 118 countries and territories joined the symbolic switch-off in support of the world’s largest grassroots environmental movement. People also committed a record-breaking three million hours of their time to take action for the planet.
